body_markdown:
## Weekly highlights


## **Ocean rates –**[Freightos Baltic Index](https://app.terminal.freightos.com/fbx)


- **Asia-US West Coast** prices (FBX01 Weekly) increased 3%.
- **Asia-US East Coast** prices (FBX03 Weekly) increased 1%.
- **Asia-N. Europe** prices (FBX11 Weekly) stayed level.
- **Asia-Mediterranean** prices (FBX13 Weekly) decreased 1%.


## **Air rates –**[Freightos Air Index](https://app.terminal.freightos.com/fax)


- **China – N. America** weekly prices increased 16%.
- **China – N. Europe** weekly prices increased 4%.
- **N. Europe – N. America** weekly prices increased 12%.


## **Analysis**


Air cargo networks in the US[are recovering](https://www.aircargonews.net/cargo-airport/2026/11/us-air-cargo-supply-chains-recover-following-ground-stop/) from the major disruption over the weekend.


Though the air traffic control system failure[grounded thousands of flights](https://www.wsj.com/business/airlines/faa-groundstop-cost-7a7e22c3) and is likely to cause some delays for air freight, international air rates to the US – which were already climbing on peak season demand for many lanes – have not surged significantly as a result.


Freightos Air Index China – N. America prices increased 16% to $9.25/kg last week but have not climbed further since the outage. This rate is already well above 2025’s peak season high of $8.00/kg reached only in mid-December last year. Seasonal volumes are layering on top of already-elevated demand and tight space due to data center buildouts.


Transatlantic rates climbed 12% to an average of $3.27/kg last week, and likewise have not moved significantly higher since the communications failure. Europe-US peak season demand is likely combining with Asia-origin volumes seeking space on alternative lanes to provide demand side pressure. Meanwhile, capacity reductions from winter schedules, and freighter shifts to higher volume lanes may also be helping push spot prices to their highest since December 2022.


In ocean freight, container carriers[continue to march back](https://www.maersk.com/news/articles/2026/11/16/structural-changes-ae1-ae2-ae3-gemini-trans-suez) to the Red Sea on Asia-Europe lanes. Together with the[rapidly growing global fleet](https://splash247.com/containership-orderbook-heads-towards-16m-teu/) , the Red Sea rebound increases the likelihood of an overcapacity challenge for carriers – and downward pressure on rates across lanes – next year.


For now though, bolstered by lingering congestion and higher fuel costs, Asia – Europe container prices are 40% – 50% higher than a year ago. Asia – N. Europe rates were level at about $3,400/FEU last week and are down 5% compared to the end of October. Asia – Mediterranean prices were also about steady at $4,300/FEU.


This stability shows that start of month GRIs did not succeed and suggest that[plans for mid-month increases](https://theloadstar.com/blanked-sailings-on-the-rise-with-container-spot-rates-on-a-gentle-decline/) may also not take, though carriers are increasing blanked sailings during this demand lull, and labor strikes in[France](https://mykn.kuehne-nagel.com/news/article/french-public-sector-unions-call-nationwide) and[Spain](https://theloadstar.com/spanish-box-terminals-face-cargo-backlog-after-general-strike/) may help absorb some capacity. Carriers are announcing increases for December too, and these price bumps could be more likely to materialize if supported by pre-Lunar New Year demand.


Transpacific rates are still at about at peak levels with prices ticking up slightly last week to $8,460/FEU to the West Coast and $9,850/FEU to the East Coast even as we enter the second half of November. Delays for containers moving inland by rail[remain a problem](https://www.joc.com/article/record-asia-imports-bnsf-woes-worsen-southern-california-rail-dwells-6323692) at LA/Long Beach, even as the ILWU Local 26’s November 20th strike deadline approaches.


President Trump is set to meet with China’s Xi Jinping this week with the interim China-US trade agreement set to expire on January 10th. Though the two states seemed set on a course for further deescalation and may still be most likely to take that path, multiple recent factors – the midterm elections, new[faces and debates](https://www.wsj.com/world/china/trumps-advisers-are-at-war-over-china-ahead-of-xi-summit-90995398) in the White House, the Nvidia scandal and new[controls over Chinese access](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/us-moves-to-limit-remote-access-to-advanced-ai-chips) to advanced US chips – are creating more tension and less certainty around where the relationship goes from here.


Finally, lower than normal rainfall in Panama over the summer triggered draft and daily transit restrictions for Panama Canal crossings, with container carriers rolling out surcharges for impacted lanes. Better than expected precipitation since then, however, has allowed the[Panama Canal Authority now to reverse](https://pancanal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ADV-42-2026-Increase-in-the-Number-of-Booking-Slots-at-the-Panamax-Locks-and-in-the-Maximum-Allowable-Draft-at-the-Neopanamax-Locks-.pdf) those steps.


Even so, expectations for a coming El Nino could still mean that restrictions will be reintroduced in the coming months. But with current[water levels](https://evtms-rpts.pancanal.com/eng/h2o/index.html) about back to normal for this time of year, the[latest projections downgrading the severity](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-12/super-el-nino-s-odds-of-being-worst-ever-are-edging-lower-us-cpc-says) of the El Nino, and expectations that next year’s[rainy season could be strong](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-12/super-el-nino-s-odds-of-being-worst-ever-are-edging-lower-us-cpc-says) and start on time, the risk of severe disruptions from canal restrictions in Q4 and through the first half of 2027 may be lower now than feared over the summer.
